source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 21 (PDF 169-185, printed 169-185); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 21 (Immunity), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Besides infections, the immune system of vertebrates defends the body against:
blocks.explanation: Vertebrates possess the immune system to defend against infections and against cancers (21.1).

book_ref.quote: To defend against infections and against cancers, vertebrates possess a defence system

blocks.prompt: 2 The chapter names which disease as very dangerous because it weakens the immune system?
blocks.explanation: Diseases that weaken the immune system, such as AIDS, are very dangerous (21.1).

book_ref.quote: That is why, the diseases that weaken the immune system, such as AIDS, are very dangerous

blocks.prompt: 3 Microbial infections, the cause of most human diseases, are invasions of the body by:

options.text: viruses, pathogenic bacteria, fungi or protists
allergens such as pollen and dust

blocks.explanation: Most human diseases result from microbial infections: invasions by viruses, pathogenic bacteria, fungi or protists (21.1).

book_ref.quote: invasions of the body by viruses, pathogenic bacteria, fungi, or protists

blocks.prompt: 4 Which of the following is NOT a part of the first line of defence?
blocks.explanation: The first line consists of skin, the digestive tract and the respiratory tract; inflammation belongs to the second line (21.1, 21.2).

book_ref.quote: The first line of defence against infections consists of skin

blocks.prompt: 5 The epidermis of human skin is how many cells thick?
blocks.explanation: The epidermis of skin is 10 to 30 cells thick (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The epidermis of skin is 10 to 30 cells thick.

blocks.prompt: 6 The outer layer of the epidermis, whose cells are continuously shed, is called:
blocks.explanation: The outer layer of epidermis is the stratum corneum; its cells are continuously shed (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The outer layer of epidermis is called stratum corneum.

blocks.prompt: 7 The cells of the stratum corneum are continuously shed because they are:
blocks.explanation: Its cells are continuously shed because they are continuously damaged (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Its cells are continuously shed, because they are continuously damaged.

blocks.prompt: 8 New skin cells that replace the worn-out cells are formed in the:
blocks.explanation: New cells are formed in the deep epidermis, migrate upward and replace worn-out cells (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: New cells are formed in the deep epidermis from where they migrate upward

blocks.prompt: 9 The protein that makes the skin tough and impenetrable for microbes is:
blocks.explanation: Skin cells form keratin protein, which makes the skin tough and impenetrable for microbes (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: These cells form keratin protein which makes the skin tough and impenetrable for microbes.

blocks.prompt: 10 Oil and sweat glands lower the pH at the skin's surface to:
blocks.explanation: Oil and sweat glands lower the skin-surface pH to 3-5, an acid level that inhibits many microbes (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The oil and sweat glands present in skin lower the pH

blocks.prompt: 11 The lysozyme present in sweat acts on:
blocks.explanation: Sweat contains lysozyme, which attacks and digests the cell walls of many bacteria (21.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Sweat also contains the enzyme lysozyme, which attacks and digests the cell walls of many bacteria.

blocks.prompt: 12 In an adult human, skin makes up what percentage of the total body weight?
blocks.explanation: Skin is the largest organ; in an adult human 15% of the total weight is skin (21.1.1, For Information).

book_ref.quote: In an adult human, 15% of the total weight is skin.

blocks.prompt: 13 The largest organ of the vertebrate body is the:
blocks.explanation: Skin is the largest organ of the vertebrate body (21.1.1, For Information).

book_ref.quote: Skin is the largest organ of the vertebrate body.

blocks.text: 21.1.2 Defence Provided by Digestive and Respiratory Tracts

blocks.prompt: 14 Most bacteria present in the food we eat are killed in the oral cavity by:
blocks.explanation: Most food bacteria are killed by saliva in the oral cavity, which also contains lysozyme (21.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Most of these are killed by saliva in the oral cavity, which also contains lysozyme.

blocks.prompt: 15 In the intestine, bacteria in food are killed by:
blocks.explanation: Strong acids of the stomach and protein-digesting enzymes in the intestine also kill bacteria (21.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The strong digestive acids present in the stomach and the protein-digesting enzymes

blocks.prompt: 16 Many bacteria in the air are trapped, before they enter the air passageway, by ciliated epithelial cells in the:
blocks.explanation: Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria before they can enter the air passageway (21.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria

blocks.prompt: 17 The sticky secretion of cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles, which traps microbes, is:
blocks.explanation: These cells secrete a layer of sticky mucus that traps microbes before they reach the lungs (21.1.2; book correction: the noun is mucus).

book_ref.quote: The cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles secrete a layer of sticky

blocks.prompt: 18 The mucus with trapped microbes is swept upward by cilia, where it:
blocks.explanation: Cilia continually sweep the mucus upward, where it can be swallowed (21.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Cilia on the cells lining these passages continually sweep

blocks.prompt: 19 The second line of defence comes into play when invaders:

options.text: overcome the first line and reach deep tissues
are trapped in the nasal cavity

blocks.explanation: When invaders overcome the first line and reach deep tissues, the second line comes into play (21.2).

book_ref.quote: When such invaders reach deep tissues, a second line of defence comes into play.

blocks.prompt: 20 Along with the first line, the second line of defence is categorized as:
blocks.explanation: Along with the first line, the second line is also a non-specific defence (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Along with the first line of defence, the second line is also categorized as a non-specific defence.

blocks.prompt: 21 Which of these is NOT one of the four most important devices of the second line of defence?
blocks.explanation: The four are germ-killer cells of blood, antimicrobial proteins, the inflammatory response and the temperature response; antibodies belong to the third line (21.2).

book_ref.quote: The four most important of these are; the germ-killer cells of blood

blocks.prompt: 22 The most important non-specific defence is provided by:
blocks.explanation: The most important non-specific defence is provided by the germ-killer cells of the blood (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: The most important non-specific defence is provided by the germ-killer cell of the blood.

blocks.prompt: 23 Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic kinds of germ-killer cells of blood?
blocks.explanation: The three basic kinds are macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells (21.2.1); plasma cells come from B cells.

book_ref.quote: There are three basic kinds: macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells.

blocks.prompt: 24 Macrophages develop from:
blocks.explanation: Macrophages develop from monocytes, a type of white blood cells (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Macrophages develop from monocytes (a type of white blood cells).

blocks.prompt: 25 A macrophage takes in a bacterium by:
blocks.explanation: A macrophage ingests a bacterium by endocytosis and kills it by its lysozyme enzymes (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: A macrophage ingests a bacterium, by endocytosis

blocks.prompt: 26 Fixed macrophages are found in all of these organs EXCEPT:
blocks.explanation: Some macrophages are fixed in organs such as lungs, liver, spleen and brain (21.2.1); the heart is not listed.

book_ref.quote: Some macrophages are fixed within some organs e.g., lungs, liver, spleen, and brain.

blocks.prompt: 27 Most macrophages:

options.text: patrol in the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid

blocks.explanation: Most macrophages patrol in the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: But most of them patrol in the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid.

blocks.prompt: 28 The network of DNA fibres released by neutrophils:

options.text: punctures the membranes of virus-infected cells
binds with pathogenic bacteria and kills them

blocks.explanation: In their third method neutrophils release a network of DNA fibres that bind with pathogenic bacteria and kill them (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: These fibres bind with pathogenic bacteria and kill them.

blocks.prompt: 29 In their second method of killing pathogens, neutrophils release:
blocks.explanation: In the second method, neutrophils release soluble anti-microbial chemicals on pathogens (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: In the second method, they release soluble anti-microbial chemicals on pathogens.

blocks.prompt: 30 Natural killer cells attack:
blocks.explanation: NK cells do not kill invading microbes; they detect and attack body cells infected with viruses (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: They do not kill invading microbes, rather they detect and attack the body cells

blocks.prompt: 31 The special proteins released by natural killer cells that insert into the target cell membrane are:
blocks.explanation: NK cells release perforins, which insert into the target cell membrane and form a pore (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: They release special proteins, called perforins

blocks.prompt: 32 A target cell attacked by a natural killer cell dies because:

options.text: its DNA is cut by lysozyme
water rushes in through the pore and the cell swells and bursts

blocks.explanation: The perforin pore lets water rush into the target cell, which swells and bursts (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This pore allows water to rush into the target cell, which then swells and bursts.

blocks.prompt: 33 Natural killer cells kill cancer cells before they:
blocks.explanation: NK cells detect cancer cells and kill them before they can develop into a tumour (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: They are also able to detect cancer cells

blocks.prompt: 34 According to the corrected fact in this topic, natural killer cells are:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate defence, not T cells and not the same as cytotoxic T cells (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: In fact NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate (non-specific) defence

blocks.prompt: 35 The patrolling germ-killer cells do not attack normal body cells because these cells carry a surface marker called:
blocks.explanation: All normal body cells carry a surface protein marker, the self-protein; germ-killer cells attack only cells lacking it (21.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This protein is called self-protein.

blocks.prompt: 36 The two main groups of protective proteins of the non-specific defence are:
blocks.explanation: The protective proteins are the complement system proteins and the interferons (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Two main groups of proteins participate in the non-specific defence of the body.

blocks.prompt: 37 The proteins of the complement system are produced in the:
blocks.explanation: Special proteins produced in the liver make the complement system (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Special proteins produced in the liver make the complement system of proteins.

blocks.prompt: 38 The complement system consists of:

options.text: more than a dozen different proteins

blocks.explanation: The complement system consists of more than a dozen different proteins circulating in an inactive state (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: This system consists of more than a dozen different proteins

blocks.prompt: 39 When complement proteins encounter a microbe, they become active:

options.text: in a sequence, the first activating the second and so on

blocks.explanation: They become active in a sequence: the first protein activates the second and so on (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: When they encounter a microbe, they become active in a sequence.

blocks.prompt: 40 The membrane-attack complex (MAC) is formed by:
blocks.explanation: The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex in the plasma membrane of the microbe (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex (MAC)

blocks.prompt: 41 After the membrane-attack complex punctures a microbe's membrane:

options.text: the microbe is coated with keratin
fluids and salts move in and the microbe swells and bursts

blocks.explanation: Fluids and salts move inside the microbe, which swells and bursts (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: So, fluids and salts move inside microbe resulting in its swelling and bursting.

blocks.prompt: 42 Interferons are released by:
blocks.explanation: Interferons are released by virus-infected cells (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: They are released by virus-infected cells.

blocks.prompt: 43 Interferons released by a virus-infected cell cause nearby cells to:
blocks.explanation: Interferons cause nearby cells to enhance their anti-viral defences (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: They cause nearby cells to enhance their anti-viral defences.

blocks.prompt: 44 Interferons belong to the large class of proteins called:
blocks.explanation: Interferons belong to the cytokines, proteins that work for communication between cells (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Interferons belong to the large class of proteins known as cytokines.

blocks.prompt: 45 Besides alerting nearby cells, interferons also activate:
blocks.explanation: Interferons also activate other immune cells such as natural killer cells and macrophages (21.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Interferons also activate other immune cells, such as natural killer cells and macrophages.

blocks.prompt: 46 The chemical signals released by injured or infected cells cause the local blood vessels to:
blocks.explanation: Histamines and prostaglandins cause local expansion of blood vessels, increasing capillary blood flow (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: These chemicals cause local expansion of blood vessels.

blocks.prompt: 47 During the inflammatory response, the capillaries at the site become:
blocks.explanation: The capillaries become more permeable (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The capillaries also become more permeable.

blocks.prompt: 48 The signs of inflammation at the spot of injury or infection are:
blocks.explanation: Increased blood flow and permeability result in redness, swelling and warmth; this is inflammation (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: It results in redness, swelling and warmth at the spot.

blocks.prompt: 49 The heat at an inflamed site:

options.text: makes the site unfavourable for microbial growth

blocks.explanation: The heat makes the site unfavourable for microbial growth, promotes healing and raises mobility of white blood cells (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The heat makes the site unfavourable for microbial growth.

blocks.prompt: 50 The phagocytes that migrate from blood to the inflamed tissue to engulf microbes are:
blocks.explanation: More phagocytes (macrophages and neutrophils) migrate to the inflamed tissue and engulf microbes (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: More phagocytes (macrophages and neutrophils) migrate from the blood to the inflamed tissue

blocks.prompt: 51 In the inflammatory response, dead microbes, cells and debris are cleaned up by:
blocks.explanation: Monocytes arrive and release chemicals to kill microbes, then macrophages clean up dead microbes, cells and debris (21.2.3).

book_ref.quote: then macrophages clean up dead microbes, cells, and debris

blocks.prompt: 52 Pus associated with some infections is a mixture of:

options.text: dead or dying neutrophils, broken down tissue cells and dead pathogens

blocks.explanation: Pus is a mixture of dead or dying neutrophils, broken down tissue cells and dead pathogens (21.2.3, For Information).

book_ref.quote: The pus associated with some infections is a mixture of dead or dying neutrophils

blocks.prompt: 53 Pyrogens act on the part of the brain that is the body's thermostat, the:
blocks.explanation: Pyrogens pass through the bloodstream to the brain and reach the hypothalamus, the body's thermostat (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: The pyrogens pass through the bloodstream to the brain and reach the hypothalamus.

blocks.prompt: 54 The normal value of the body's core temperature, above which pyrogens raise it, is:
blocks.explanation: Pyrogens stimulate the hypothalamus to raise the core temperature above the normal 37 °C (98.6 °F) (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: Here, the pyrogens stimulate the hypothalamus to boost the body

blocks.prompt: 55 Another name for fever is:
blocks.explanation: The higher-than-normal temperature is known as fever (pyrexia) (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: The higher-than-normal temperature is known as fever (pyrexia).

blocks.prompt: 56 Fever acts as a defence mechanism because it:

options.text: hinders the ability of bacteria and viruses to reproduce

blocks.explanation: Fever hinders the ability of bacteria and viruses to reproduce (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: It hinders the ability of bacteria and viruses to reproduce.

blocks.prompt: 57 Which of these is named in the chapter as a temperature-sensitive microbe killed at high fever?
blocks.explanation: Some microbes, e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae and influenza, are temperature-sensitive and are killed at high fever (21.2.4; book correction: pneumoniae).

book_ref.quote: are temperature-sensitive and are killed at high fever

blocks.prompt: 58 During fever, the actions of which cells become faster?
blocks.explanation: Fever enhances the speed of the actions of neutrophils and macrophages (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: Fever also enhances the speed of the actions of neutrophils and macrophages.

blocks.prompt: 59 Body temperatures greater than which value are often fatal?
blocks.explanation: Temperatures greater than 103 °F (39.4 °C) are dangerous and those greater than 105 °F (40.5 °C) are often fatal (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: and those greater than 105

blocks.prompt: 60 During fever, the body releases more:
blocks.explanation: During fever the body releases more cytokines (interferons) (21.2.4).

book_ref.quote: During fever, the body releases more cytokines (interferons).

blocks.prompt: 61 The third line of defence is called specific because it:

options.text: acts the same way against all germs
is present only on the skin
targets specific germs and acts especially against them

blocks.explanation: The third line is the specific defence: it targets specific germs and acts especially against them (21.3).

book_ref.quote: It is the specific defence, which means that it targets specific germs

blocks.prompt: 62 A feature of the third line of defence that the first two lines lack is that it:

options.text: remembers previous invaders and responds quickly to them

blocks.explanation: The immune system can remember previous invaders and responds quickly if they enter again (21.3).

book_ref.quote: can remember previous invaders and responds quickly if they enter the body again

blocks.prompt: 63 The non-specific defence present at birth is also called:
blocks.explanation: Non-specific defence is present at birth, so it is called inborn or innate immunity (Types of Immunity).

book_ref.quote: So, it is also called inborn or innate immunity.

blocks.prompt: 64 The specific defence that develops during growth is called:
blocks.explanation: The specific defence is acquired during growth and is called acquired immunity (Types of Immunity).

book_ref.quote: While the specific defence is acquired during growth and it is called acquired immunity.

blocks.prompt: 65 In passive immunity:

options.text: the individual is given antibodies against specific microbes

blocks.explanation: In passive immunity the individual is given antibodies to combat specific microbes; it is short-lived (Types of Immunity).

book_ref.quote: While, in passive immunity, the individual is given antibodies to combat specific microbes.

blocks.prompt: 66 The most effective form of immunity is:
blocks.explanation: In natural active immunity the body prepares antibodies naturally when exposed to antigens; it is the most effective form (Types of Immunity).

book_ref.quote: It is the most effective form of immunity.

blocks.prompt: 67 Artificial active immunity is achieved by:
blocks.explanation: Artificial active immunity is achieved by giving weakened antigens (vaccination), which stimulate the body to prepare antibodies (Types of Immunity).

book_ref.quote: Artificial active immunity is achieved by administering weakened antigens in the body (vaccination).

blocks.prompt: 68 The immune system is best described as:

options.text: a single organ in the chest
a gland located in the neck
many individual cells that rush to the infection site
the outer layer of the skin

blocks.explanation: The immune system is not localized; it is composed of many individual cells that rush to the infection site (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The immune system is not localized to one place in the body.

blocks.prompt: 69 T cells and B cells together are called:
blocks.explanation: T and B cells are collectively called lymphocytes (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: T and B cells are collectively called lymphocytes.

blocks.prompt: 70 The three main kinds of white blood cells forming the immune system are:

options.text: monocytes, T cells and B cells
neutrophils, mast cells and plasma cells
B cells, mast cells and myelomas

blocks.explanation: There are three main kinds: monocytes, T cells and B cells (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: There are three main kinds of white blood cells i.e., monocytes, T cells, and B cells.

blocks.prompt: 71 When monocytes enter the interstitial fluid, they mature into:
blocks.explanation: Monocytes circulate in blood, enter the interstitial fluid and mature into macrophages (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Here, they mature into macrophages.

blocks.prompt: 72 The macrophages formed from monocytes produce proteins that activate:
blocks.explanation: Macrophages phagocytose microbes and also produce proteins that activate the helper T cells (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: They also produce proteins that activate the helper T cells.

blocks.prompt: 73 According to the corrected fact, monocytes are produced in the:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: monocytes, like other white blood cells, are produced in the bone marrow from myeloid stem cells (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: are produced in the bone marrow, from myeloid stem cells

blocks.prompt: 74 Besides phagocytosis, monocyte-derived cells also:

options.text: clear cellular debris and assist in repairing tissue damage

blocks.explanation: They help to clear cellular debris and assist in repairing tissue damage (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: They also help to clear cellular debris and assist in repairing tissue damage.

blocks.prompt: 75 T cells mature in the thymus, which is:

options.text: a large gland below the stomach
a part of the bone marrow
a small grey gland located just above the heart

blocks.explanation: T cells migrate to the thymus, a small grey gland just above the heart, where they mature (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: They migrate to the thymus, a small grey gland located just above the heart.

blocks.prompt: 76 Each T cell is specialized to recognize:
blocks.explanation: Each T cell is specialized in recognizing one particular antigen; tens of millions of different T cells are made (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Each T cell is specialized in recognizing one particular antigen.

blocks.prompt: 77 The T cells that supervise the development of T cells in the thymus are:
blocks.explanation: Inducer T cells supervise the development of T cells in the thymus (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Inducer T cells, which supervise the development of T cells in the thymus

blocks.prompt: 78 The T cells that terminate the immune response are:
blocks.explanation: Suppressor T cells terminate the immune response (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Suppressor T cells, which terminate the immune response

blocks.prompt: 79 B cells complete their maturation in the:
blocks.explanation: Unlike T cells, B cells do not travel to the thymus; they complete their maturation in the bone marrow (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: They complete their maturation in the bone marrow.

blocks.prompt: 80 The antibody produced by each plasma cell:

options.text: sticks to the antigen, marking it for destruction

blocks.explanation: Each plasma cell produces an antibody that sticks to the antigen, marking it for destruction (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Each plasma cell produces an antibody that sticks to the antigen, marking it for destruction.

blocks.prompt: 81 When microbes attack the body, the immediate response is provided by:
blocks.explanation: Macrophages provide the immediate response by engulfing microbes, giving time for the immune system to respond (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: macrophages provide the immediate response by engulfing them

blocks.prompt: 82 Helper T cells are activated when their receptors recognize:

options.text: special proteins produced by a macrophage that has engulfed a microbe

blocks.explanation: A macrophage that engulfs a microbe produces special proteins; helper T cells recognize them through receptors and are activated (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: When the helper T cells recognize these proteins through their receptors, they are activated.

blocks.prompt: 83 Activated helper T cells initiate:

options.text: two parallel responses: cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immunity

blocks.explanation: Activated helper T cells initiate two parallel immune responses: cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immunity (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The activated helper T cells initiate two parallel immune responses

blocks.prompt: 84 Cytotoxic T cells kill infected or cancer cells by:

options.text: puncturing the membranes of the target cells

blocks.explanation: Their mechanism is the same as that of NK cells: they puncture the membranes of host target cells (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Their mechanism of killing is the same as that of natural killer cells

blocks.prompt: 85 In cell-mediated immunity, T cell growth factor produced by an activated helper T cell:

options.text: starts proliferation of all types of T cells, forming large clones

blocks.explanation: Proliferation: T cell growth factor starts the proliferation of all types of T cells, forming large clones (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: it produces soluble chemicals e.g., T cell growth factor

blocks.prompt: 86 The event of cell-mediated immunity in which a second factor from the helper T cell attracts macrophages to the infection site is:
blocks.explanation: Activation: a second factor secreted by the activated helper T cell attracts macrophages to the site of infection (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: A second factor is secreted by the activated helper T cell, which attracts macrophages

blocks.prompt: 87 In the event called induction, helper T cells activate:

options.text: B cells in the bone marrow
inducer T cells in the thymus

blocks.explanation: Induction: helper T cells activate inducer T cells in the thymus, which trigger maturation of lymphocytes into T cells (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Helper T cells activate inducer T cells in the thymus

blocks.prompt: 88 Suppressor T cells cannot block the cytotoxic attack at the start because:

options.text: they live only in the skin

blocks.explanation: Suppressor T cells multiply more slowly than cytotoxic T cells; their low initial numbers prevent them from blocking the attack (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Their low initial numbers prevent them from blocking the cytotoxic attack.

blocks.prompt: 89 Suppressor T cells become numerous enough to shut down the cytotoxic T cell response after about:
blocks.explanation: After 1 to 2 weeks the number of suppressor T cells rises enough to shut down the cytotoxic T cell response (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: After 1 to 2 weeks, however, the number of suppressor T cells rises

blocks.prompt: 90 The helper and cytotoxic T cells that persist after suppression, probably for life, are called:
blocks.explanation: After suppression a population of T cells persists; these helper and cytotoxic T cells are memory cells giving a rapid response later (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: These helper and cytotoxic T cells are now called memory cells.

blocks.prompt: 91 Antibody-mediated immunity is also called:
blocks.explanation: The second, stronger defence is called antibody-mediated or humoral immunity (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: called antibody-mediated or humoral immunity

blocks.prompt: 92 In antibody-mediated immunity, B cells:

options.text: mark antigens for destruction and inactivate toxic molecules

blocks.explanation: B cells do not attack antigens directly; they mark them for destruction and inactivate toxic molecules (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: They do not attack the antigens directly. Rather, they mark them for destruction.

blocks.prompt: 93 A B cell binds to antigens through:

options.text: B receptor proteins on its surface

blocks.explanation: Each B cell binds to antigens through the B receptor proteins on its surface (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Each B cell binds to the antigens through the B receptor proteins on its surface.

blocks.prompt: 94 When plasma cells secrete their B receptor proteins, these are called:
blocks.explanation: Plasma cells produce more B receptor proteins, which are secreted and now called antibodies (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The B receptor proteins are secreted and now called as antibodies.

blocks.prompt: 95 Antibodies make up about what percentage by weight of the total protein in blood plasma?
blocks.explanation: Antibodies constitute about 20% by weight of the total protein in blood plasma (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Antibodies constitute about 20% by weight of the total protein in blood plasma.

blocks.prompt: 96 Vaccines are made from:
blocks.explanation: Vaccines are made from killed or weakened pathogens; they stimulate antibody production and memory cells (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Vaccines are made from killed or weakened pathogens that cause antibody production.

blocks.prompt: 97 Which of these is NOT one of the three mechanisms by which antibody-marked antigens are destroyed?

options.text: Release of pyrogens by mast cells

blocks.explanation: The three mechanisms are complement, macrophages and killer cells (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Rather, they mark it for destruction by one of three mechanisms.

blocks.prompt: 98 Killer cells of antibody-mediated immunity differ from natural killer cells in that they:

options.text: possess receptors that recognize antibody-coated antigens

blocks.explanation: Killer cells are similar to NK cells except that they possess receptors that recognize antibody-coated antigens (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Killer cells are similar to natural killer cells, except that these possess receptors

blocks.prompt: 99 The antibody response is shut down after several weeks by:
blocks.explanation: After several weeks, the suppressor T cells shut down the antibody response (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: After several weeks, the suppressor T cells shut down the antibody response.

blocks.prompt: 100 According to the corrected fact, memory B cells come from:

options.text: the clone of activated B cells, some of which do not become plasma cells
plasma cells that stop secreting antibodies

blocks.explanation: Book correction: plasma cells are end cells; memory B cells come from activated B cells of the clone that do not become plasma cells (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: memory B cells come from the clone of activated B cells

blocks.prompt: 101 In the gene therapy approach for malignant melanoma, TIL is engineered to make:
blocks.explanation: Genetic engineers are trying to insert a gene into TIL enabling it to make tumour necrosis factor, which kills tumour cells (21.3.2, box).

book_ref.quote: The gene will enable TIL to make a protein called tumour necrosis factor (TNF).

blocks.prompt: 102 An antibody molecule is composed of:

options.text: one heavy and one light chain
two heavy and two light polypeptide chains

blocks.explanation: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein of four polypeptide chains: two identical heavy chains and two light chains (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: It is composed of four polypeptide chains

blocks.prompt: 103 The four chains of an antibody are held together by:
